title: Quantum Key Distribution Beyond Stationary Channels
authors: Vaisakh Mannalath, Víctor Zapatero, Kiyoshi Tamaki, Marcos Curty
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) over non-stationary channels, such as satellite links, is characterized by short, high-loss, and strongly fluctuating transmission windows that produce sparse detection events. In many QKD protocols, these data must be analyzed using non-IID statistical inequalities, yet existing methods either become loose for small sample sizes or heavily rely on fine-tuning, yielding poor estimates when the optical channel is mis-modeled. Using mixture martingale techniques, we introduce tight concentration inequalities that retain sharpness when the channel model is accurate, while remaining robust to model mismatch. In realistic simulations of satellite QKD with fluctuating loss, the resulting bounds can reduce the minimum required number of transmitted signals by more than $70\%$.
summary: This paper introduces mixture martingale techniques to derive robust concentration inequalities for QKD over highly variable channels like satellite links. By applying these bounds to finite key rate estimation, the authors demonstrate that their method significantly improves the achievable secure key rate compared to standard theoretical limits when channel losses are mis-modeled.
main_problem: The core problem is accurately estimating the finite secret key rate for Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) over non-stationary channels, particularly satellite links.
main_result: The proposed mixture-martingale bounds significantly outperform existing concentration inequalities like Kato's bound, especially when the actual channel loss deviates from the expected model value.
method: The authors develop and apply mixture martingale techniques to derive tight concentration inequalities for non-IID random variables arising from QKD measurements.
model_or_system: The study models Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) using the decoy-state BB84 protocol over simulated satellite links (LEO/GEO). These channels are characterized by short, high-loss, and strongly fluctuating transmission windows.
key_observables: Finite secret key rate ($\ell$), upper bounds on statistical gaps ($\mu$ or $\Lambda$), and error probabilities ($P_{	ext{err}Z}, P_{	ext{err}X}$).
important_parameters: Channel loss mismatch (e.g., 35 dB vs 30 dB), failure probability ($\epsilon=10^{-20}$), and the number of transmitted signals ($N$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that standard methods fail due to sensitivity to model mismatch, necessitating robust bounds like the mixture martingale approach.
figures_summary: Figures compare the finite secret key rate versus the number of rounds (N) for LEO and GEO links under varying observed loss mismatches, showing the superior performance of the union/mixture-martingale bounds relative to other theoretical limits.
paper_structure: The paper develops general mixture-martingale concentration inequalities first, then applies these tools to benchmark finite key rate estimation for decoy-state BB84 protocols across various simulated satellite channel loss mismatches.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous mathematical tools (mixture martingales) to analyze the performance limits of quantum communication systems under realistic, non-ideal environmental conditions like fluctuating atmospheric or free-space optical links.
